newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Strong cash underpins BICC results.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Strong cash underpins BICC results.

text.p: British cable manufacturer and civil engineer BICC plc reported steady 1996 results on Wednesday, underpinned by strong cash, but warned of weakness remaining in some of its core markets.
Investors took little heart from the figures, despite an 18 percent rise in pretax profits to 129 million pounds ($207.9 million).
In a broadly weaker London stock market BICC shares dropped 8.0 pence to 271-1/2 pence by 1245 GMT.

However, chief executive Alan Jones told Reuters in a telephone interview after the results that he was especially pleased with year-end net debt of 80 million pounds that was "about half what the city expected".

These gains stemmed from good cash efficiency in the year and, coupled with the resources provided by a 170 million pound rights issue last year, meant the group was poised to increase capital expenditure by about 40 percent in 1997 for the second year running.

Jones described this ongoing reorganisation and redirection of capital as "a reinvestment phase" --tied to a plan designed to forge new growth from cables in the developing economies of Asia and Latin America.

Across cables and construction, BICC has consolidated its businesses in developed markets and sought to reduce exposure and tied-up capital in low margin sectors -- creating more room for a big push into data and communications cables, as well as into railway services.

However, Jones noted that weakness in the traditional power cable product market in Europe was a source of worry, at least for the first half of 1997, and the outlook for its big civil engineering unit Balfour Beatty was one of only gradual profit improvement.

No further major closures or reductions were expected in traditional cables in Europe, he said, adding that Balfour Beatty had now pulled out of general construction in the United States but retained a strong business in heavy civil engineering there.

Jones said he still believed that the redirection of investment into new growth areas would pay off soon, noting that the group expects improvements in these to continue "with an emphasis on the second half".
The plan has been helped along by the "encouragingly better" cash performance which he said reflected tighter management and got some help from exchange rates and copper prices.

"With our improved financial position, we are continuing with investments in these business sectors with considerable capital expenditure in 1997. These projects will be completed in 1997 and 1998 and will contribute to further growth," the group said.
The group said it would pay a final dividend of 8.5 pence to give a total for the year of 12.5 pence per share. ($ = 0.620 British Pounds)
